Algebra I · Lesson 2.3

Factoring Out a Common Factor

Solve this lesson →All lessons

The distributive property turns a(b+c)a(b+c) into ab+acab+ac. This lesson runs that rule backward. Reading ab+acab+ac as a(b+c)a(b+c) is called factoring, and the first problems are pure arithmetic, with no letters in them at all.

Problem
Compute 57⋅69+57⋅3157⋅69+57⋅31 without working out either product. Both terms contain the factor 5757, so pull it out front and see what the leftover sum becomes.
Show a hint
  • The first term is 5757 copies of 6969, and the second is 5757 more copies of 3131. Count copies before multiplying anything.
Show the full solution
Both terms share 5757, so pull it out front. 57⋅69+57⋅31=57(69+31)=57⋅100=5700.57⋅69+57⋅31=57(69+31)=57⋅100=5700​. Counting copies beats multiplying here, since the leftovers add to a round 100100.
Key idea
Factoring. Reading ab+acab+ac as a(b+c)a(b+c) is called factoring. It is the distributive property used right to left. Expanding removes parentheses, and factoring adds them. Both moves use the same equality. Factoring rewrites a sum of products as a single product. In the last problem it rewrote 5757 copies of 6969 plus 5757 copies of 3131 as 5757 copies of 100100, a one-step computation.
Problem
Compute 58⋅91−58⋅8158⋅91−58⋅81 the same way. The shared factor comes out front, and this time a subtraction is left behind it. What is the value of the whole expression?
Show a hint
  • The first product is 5858 copies of 9191 and the second is 5858 copies of 8181, so subtracting leaves 5858 copies of some difference.
Show the full solution
Pull the shared 5858 out front and the subtraction stays inside. 58⋅91−58⋅81=58(91−81)=58⋅10=580.58⋅91−58⋅81=58(91−81)=58⋅10=580​. The long way, 5278−46985278−4698, reaches the same 580580 with far more work.
Key idea
Expand back to check. The subtraction form ab−ac=a(b−c)ab−ac=a(b−c) is not a second law, since 1.3 made subtracting cc the same as adding −c−c. Expand every proposed factoring back and compare it to the original. That check is the round trip. Since 2.1 made you fluent at expanding, you can always grade your own work. The match must be exact, every term and every sign, or the factoring is wrong. The slip it catches most often is dividing only the first term by the shared factor, and one expansion shows it.
Problem
Letters change nothing. The expression 4w+364w+36 factors as 4(w+c)4(w+c) for one constant cc. Divide each term by the shared 44, then enter cc.
Show a hint
  • Both terms get divided by the 44, not just the first one.
Show the full solution
Divide both terms by 44. Since 4w÷4=w4w÷4=w and 36÷4=936÷4=9, the factoring is 4(w+9)4(w+9), so c=9c=9​. Expanding 4(w+9)4(w+9) lands back on 4w+364w+36. Dividing only the first term gives 4(w+36)4(w+36), which expands to 4w+1444w+144 instead.
Key idea
How to factor. Find a factor shared by every term, divide each term by it, and write the leftovers inside the parentheses. Each leftover keeps the sign of the term it came from, so a negative term leaves a negative leftover. Finding the shared factor means scanning each term's factors, the parts vocabulary from 1.4, and looking for one that shows up in every term. Then expand your answer, and it has to reproduce the original exactly.
Problem
Dana factors 12h+3012h+30 as 2(6h+15)2(6h+15), and expanding it back checks out. But inside the parentheses, 6h6h and 1515 still share a factor, so the job is unfinished. Enter the largest number that divides both 12h12h and 3030.
Show a hint
  • What is the largest number that divides both 1212 and 3030?
Show the full solution
Since gcd⁡(12,30)=6gcd(12,30)=6, the largest number dividing both terms is 66​, and the complete factoring is 6(2h+5)6(2h+5). Dana's 2(6h+15)2(6h+15) expands back correctly, so passing the round trip does not mean the job is finished. Check whether the leftovers still share a factor.
Key idea
Factor completely. An expression is factored completely once the leftovers inside the parentheses share nothing but 11. A partial factoring like 2(6h+15)2(6h+15) passes the round trip, since it really does equal 12h+3012h+30. Completeness needs its own check. Look at the leftovers, and if they still share a factor bigger than 11, pull that out too. The number part of the largest common factor is the GCD from Prealgebra 3.5, so gcd⁡(12,30)=6gcd(12,30)=6 gives the complete factoring 6(2h+5)6(2h+5) in one step.
Problem
A letter can be the shared factor. Since y2y2 means y⋅yy⋅y (1.5), both terms of y2+10yy2+10y contain yy, so the expression factors as y(y+c)y(y+c). Enter cc.
Show a hint
  • Divide each term by yy and see what each one leaves behind.
Show the full solution
Divide each term by yy. Since y2÷y=yy2÷y=y and 10y÷y=1010y÷y=10, the factoring is y(y+10)y(y+10), and the round trip y(y+10)=y2+10yy(y+10)=y2+10y confirms c=10c=10​. The terms share no number bigger than 11, but a shared letter is a common factor too.
Problem
Number and letter combine. Enter the greatest common factor of the two terms of 8t2+20t8t2+20t, typed like a term, for example 6z6z.
Show a hint
  • Find the number part and the letter part separately, then put them together.
Show the full solution
The number part is gcd⁡(8,20)=4gcd(8,20)=4, and both terms contain one tt, so the greatest common factor is 4t4t​. Pulling it out gives 4t(2t+5)4t(2t+5). Answering just 44 or just tt stops halfway, since the shared factor carries a number and a letter.
Key idea
Greatest common factor of terms. The greatest common factor of a set of terms has two parts, the GCD of the number parts and every letter all the terms share. Pulling 4t4t out of 8t2+20t8t2+20t leaves 2t+52t+5. Since 2t2t and 55 share nothing but 11, the factoring is complete. One expansion, 4t(2t+5)=8t2+20t4t(2t+5)=8t2+20t, confirms it.
Problem
A student factors 8n+368n+36 as 4(2n+8)4(2n+8). Test it the 1.4 way, evaluate the original and the claimed factoring at n=1n=1, each on its own. How far apart are their values?
Show a hint
  • Work out each expression at n=1n=1 separately, then subtract the results.
Show the full solution
At n=1n=1 the original gives 8+36=448+36=44 and the claimed factoring gives 4(2+8)=404(2+8)=40, so the two are 44​ apart. Expanding catches it faster, since 4(2n+8)=8n+324(2n+8)=8n+32 rather than 8n+368n+36. The 44 does divide both terms, but the leftover constant is wrong.
Key idea
Always check by expanding. A wrong factoring cannot pass the round trip. By 1.4's one-mismatch rule it also fails a single evaluation, since one input giving two different outputs proves the claim false. Expanding is the stronger check and usually the faster one. Compare one distribution against the original, term by term and sign by sign.
Problem
Three terms this time. The expression 9a+27b−189a+27b−18 factors as 9(a+3b+c)9(a+3b+c), and each term keeps its sign as the 99 comes out. Enter cc, sign included.
Show a hint
  • What is −18−18 divided by 99, sign and all?
Show the full solution
The third term is −18−18, and −18÷9=−2−18÷9=−2, so 9a+27b−18=9(a+3b−2)9a+27b−18=9(a+3b−2) and c=−2c=−2​. Each leftover keeps the sign of the term it came from, so dropping the minus would break the expansion.
Problem
In m(m−6)+8(m−6)m(m−6)+8(m−6), both terms contain the whole factor m−6m−6. Pull the chunk out front exactly the way the 5757 came out in this lesson's first problem. The result is (m+a)(m−6)(m+a)(m−6). Enter aa.
Show a hint
  • Treat m−6m−6 as a single object, like the shared 5757 in the hook problem.
  • The first term is mm copies of m−6m−6, and the second term adds some more copies of the same thing. Count the total number of copies.
Show the full solution
Treat m−6m−6 as one object. The first term is mm copies of it and the second is 88 copies, which is m+8m+8 copies in all, so the expression equals (m+8)(m−6)(m+8)(m−6) and a=8a=8​. Expanding the two products into four separate terms first would erase the shared chunk, and chapter 9 factors quadratics with this same move.
Fun fact
The padlock in your browser's address bar rests on factoring being hard. Multiplying two enormous primes takes a computer an instant, but recovering them from the product alone would outlast the age of the universe.

Factoring reads distribution backward, the round trip checks it, completeness finishes it, and even a whole parenthesized chunk can be the shared factor. Next, 2.4 adds and subtracts entire expressions, and the full sign flip from distributing −1−1 in 2.1 becomes the main skill.

Practice these ideas

Practice
Compute 34⋅67+34⋅3334⋅67+34⋅33 without working out either product. Factor out the shared 3434 first and see what sum is left behind it.
Show the solution
Both terms contain 3434, so the sum is 34(67+33)=34⋅100=340034(67+33)=34⋅100=3400​. Grinding out 2278+11222278+1122 gets there too, just slowly.
Practice
Compute 76⋅53−76⋅4376⋅53−76⋅43 by factoring first. Both products are ugly, but the difference left behind the shared factor is not.
Show the solution
Pull the shared 7676 out front, since 76(53−43)=76⋅10=76076(53−43)=76⋅10=760​. Subtracting inside the parentheses is far less work than computing 4028−32684028−3268.
Practice
The expression 5q+605q+60 factors as 5(q+c)5(q+c) for one constant cc. Divide each term by the shared 55, then enter cc.
Show the solution
Divide each term by 55. Since 5q÷5=q5q÷5=q and 60÷5=1260÷5=12, the factoring is 5(q+12)5(q+12), which expands back to 5q+605q+60, so c=12c=12​. Writing 5(q+60)5(q+60) divides only the first term and fails the round trip.
Practice
Enter the largest number that divides both terms of 38x+9538x+95. Neither number is small, so factor each one before searching for what they share.
Show the solution
Since 38=2⋅1938=2⋅19 and 95=5⋅1995=5⋅19, the largest common factor is 1919​ and the complete form is 19(2x+5)19(2x+5). Guessing small divisors stalls here, since 22 misses 9595 and 55 misses 3838. Factor each number first instead.
Practice
Ravi factors 44h+6644h+66 as 11(4h+6)11(4h+6), and the expansion checks out. Even so, 4h4h and 66 still share a factor, so the factoring is not complete. Enter the largest common factor of the two original terms.
Show the solution
Since gcd⁡(44,66)=22gcd(44,66)=22, the largest common factor is 2222​, and the complete form 22(2h+3)22(2h+3) expands back to 44h+6644h+66. Ravi's 11(4h+6)11(4h+6) also expands correctly, but its leftovers 4h4h and 66 still share 22, so it is not finished.
Practice
The shared factor is a letter this time. Since n2n2 is n⋅nn⋅n, both terms of n2+13nn2+13n contain nn, so the expression factors as n(n+c)n(n+c). Enter cc.
Show the solution
The terms share no number, but both contain nn. Dividing each by nn leaves n+13n+13, and the round trip n(n+13)=n2+13nn(n+13)=n2+13n confirms c=13c=13​.
Practice
Number and letter both matter here. Enter the greatest common factor of the two terms of 15u2+25u15u2+25u, typed like a term, for example 8w8w.
Show the solution
The number part is gcd⁡(15,25)=5gcd(15,25)=5, and both terms contain uu, so the greatest common factor is 5u5u​. Pulling it out gives 5u(3u+5)5u(3u+5). Entering only 55 or only uu stops halfway.
Practice
The expression 26x+39y−5226x+39y−52 factors as 13(2x+3y+e)13(2x+3y+e). Enter ee, sign included.
Show the solution
Since −52÷13=−4−52÷13=−4, the factoring is 13(2x+3y−4)13(2x+3y−4), which expands back to 26x+39y−5226x+39y−52, so e=−4e=−4​. Each leftover keeps the sign of its own term, so dropping the minus changes the expression.
Practice
Evaluate 7⋅93+7⋅710107⋅93+7⋅7​ without any long multiplication. The top is a sum of two products with a shared factor, so factor it before dividing anything.
Show the solution
Factor the top first, since 7⋅93+7⋅7=7(93+7)=7⋅100=7007⋅93+7⋅7=7(93+7)=7⋅100=700, and 700÷10=70700÷10=70​. The shared 77 turns two ugly products into one round number.
Practice
Both terms of d(d+5)+3(d+5)d(d+5)+3(d+5) contain the whole chunk d+5d+5, so it can come out front like any shared factor. Factoring it out gives (d+a)(d+5)(d+a)(d+5). Enter aa.
Show the solution
Count copies of the chunk d+5d+5. The first term is dd copies and the second is 33 more, so there are d+3d+3 copies in all, giving (d+3)(d+5)(d+3)(d+5) and a=3a=3​. The tempting answer 55 sits inside the shared chunk, not in the leftover factor.
Practice
One more full scan, this one on 6t2+9t6t2+9t. Enter the greatest common factor of its two terms, typed like a term. Check that the leftovers share nothing before you commit.
Show the solution
Since gcd⁡(6,9)=3gcd(6,9)=3 and both terms contain tt, the greatest common factor is 3t3t​ and the complete form is 3t(2t+3)3t(2t+3). The leftovers 2t2t and 33 share only 11, so nothing is left to pull. Stopping at 33 would leave the shared tt behind.
Practice
Evaluate 412+41412+41 by factoring before you compute anything. Done right, one clean product replaces a square plus an addition.
Show the solution
Both terms contain 4141, so 412+41=41(41+1)=41⋅42=1722412+41=41(41+1)=41⋅42=1722​. The shape is general, since n2+nn2+n always factors as n(n+1)n(n+1), a product of two consecutive whole numbers.
